blocks.text: 1. Training Loops
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205082-889572630.png

Learning Curves, the previous topic, visualized how training progresses over time. Training Loops cover the actual code structure that produces those curves, the concrete, repeated sequence of steps that trains a network.

This is the concrete, repeated sequence of steps that trains a network, tying together nearly every concept already covered throughout this module into one coherent, repeated procedure explored in full depth throughout this topic.
2. The Outer Loop
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205082-99722531.png
This connects back to Epochs, already covered in its own topic. The outer loop runs once per epoch, repeating the entire inner process, covered in the next section, for as many epochs as chosen.
This directly mirrors the epoch-versus-iteration hierarchy already covered in Iterations, with the outer loop corresponding exactly to the epoch level of that hierarchy.
3. The Inner Loop
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205082-360797721.png

This connects back to Batches and Iterations, both already covered. The inner loop runs once per batch within that epoch, nested directly inside the outer loop already covered in the previous section.
Each pass through the inner loop is genuinely one iteration, already covered, directly matching the precise terminology already established for exactly this repeated, per-batch process.

blocks.text: 4. The Four Core Steps Per Iteration

blocks.alt: The Four Core Steps Per Iteration
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205082-641935096.png

The genuinely core four steps repeated every single iteration begin with the forward pass, already covered in Forward Propagation, followed by computing the loss, already covered throughout Loss Functions.

Next comes the backward pass, already covered in Backpropagation, and finally updating weights, already covered in Gradient Descent, completing one full iteration before the inner loop moves to the next batch.
5. Zeroing Gradients Between Iterations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205082-254242268.png

A genuinely critical, real implementation detail follows. Gradients from the previous iteration must be genuinely cleared before computing new ones, a step easy to overlook but genuinely essential for correctness.
Forgetting this step genuinely accumulates gradients incorrectly across iterations, silently corrupting every subsequent weight update already covered as the fourth step in the previous section.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: This exact mistake, forgetting to zero gradients, already covered in this topic, is one of the single most common real bugs when implementing a training loop directly rather than relying on a high-level framework.

blocks.text: 6. Switching Into Training Mode
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205610-255788641.png

This connects back to Dropout and Batch Normalization, already covered in earlier modules. The network must be genuinely switched into training mode before the loop begins, a genuinely important setup step.
This ensures those techniques' own training-time behavior, already covered, actually applies, since both rely on knowing whether the network is currently in a training or inference context.
7. Validation Inside The Loop
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445205611-5033136.png

This connects back to Learning Curves, already covered in the previous topic. A validation pass typically runs once per epoch, inside the outer loop, right after that epoch's training iterations finish.

This produces exactly the validation loss values already covered as one of the two curves in the previous topic, computed without weight updates, since validation only measures performance rather than training on it.
8. Tracking Metrics Throughout The Loop
A genuinely important bookkeeping step follows. Loss and other metrics get recorded at the end of each iteration or epoch, building up a genuinely complete history of the entire training run.

This recorded history is exactly what produces the Learning Curves already covered in the previous topic, confirming the direct, concrete link between this topic's code structure and that topic's own visualizations.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why Understanding This Structure Genuinely Matters
Debugging genuinely broken or unstable training is a direct case where understanding each of the four core steps, already covered, helps pinpoint exactly where a problem originates within the loop.

Implementing training from scratch, without a high-level framework handling it automatically, is another genuine case where this exact structure, already covered throughout this topic, is what needs to be written directly.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely complete, minimal training loop, showing the outer epoch loop, the inner batch loop, and all four core steps already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 3))
true_weights = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5])
y = X @ true_weights + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=200)

weights = np.zeros(3)
learning_rate = 0.01
num_epochs = 5       # already covered in Epochs
batch_size = 32       # already covered in Batch Size

for epoch in range(num_epochs):  # the outer loop, already covered in this topic
    indices = np.arange(len(X))
    rng.shuffle(indices)  # already covered as why shuffling genuinely matters in Batches
    epoch_loss = 0.0

    for start in range(0, len(X), batch_size):  # the inner loop, already covered in this topic
        batch_indices = indices[start:start + batch_size]
        X_batch, y_batch = X[batch_indices], y[batch_indices]

        predictions = X_batch @ weights           # forward pass, already covered in this topic
        errors = predictions - y_batch
        loss = np.mean(errors ** 2)                # compute loss, already covered in this topic
        gradient = (2 / len(X_batch)) * X_batch.T @ errors  # backward pass, already covered in this topic
        weights = weights - learning_rate * gradient          # update weights, already covered in this topic

        epoch_loss += loss

    print(f"Epoch {epoch + 1}/{num_epochs}: avg loss={epoch_loss / (len(X) / batch_size):.4f}")

print("Final weights:", np.round(weights, 3), "vs true weights:", true_weights)

blocks.content: Running this example shows the loss steadily decreasing across epochs as the four core steps, already covered in this topic, repeat across every iteration within every epoch.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A training loop is the concrete, repeated sequence of steps that trains a network.
The outer loop runs once per epoch; the inner loop runs once per batch, equivalently once per iteration.
Every iteration repeats four core steps: forward pass, compute loss, backward pass, update weights.
Gradients must be zeroed between iterations to avoid incorrect accumulation.
The network must be switched into training mode so Dropout and Batch Normalization behave correctly.
A validation pass typically runs once per epoch, without updating weights.
Recording loss and metrics throughout the loop is exactly what produces Learning Curves.
Understanding this structure is essential for debugging training or implementing it from scratch.
